title: HUSBANDS WERE NOT TOLD TO CONTROL THEIR WIVES—They Were Told to Love Them as Christ Loved the Church
paragraphs: HUSBANDS WERE NOT TOLD TO CONTROL THEIR WIVES—They Were Told to Love Them as Christ Loved the Church
Somewhere along the way, some men learned how to quote “wives, submit” while forgetting that Jesus gave husbands something far more terrifying to imitate: a cross.
There is a verse some husbands know by heart.
And then there is the verse that should break their hearts.
Some can quote what Scripture says to a wife.
Some can explain “headship.”
Some can defend authority.
Some can talk about submission until everyone at the dinner table goes quiet.
But then Paul turns toward the husband.
And suddenly the standard is not his culture.
Not his father.
Not his temper.
Not his paycheck.
Not his position.
Not even another “good Christian husband.”
Paul points at Jesus Christ.
And everything changes.
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.” — Ephesians 5:25, KJV
Read it again.
Slowly.
Because buried inside that sentence is enough truth to expose generations of counterfeit masculinity.
The Greek is even harder to escape:
“Οἱ ἄνδρες, ἀγαπᾶτε τὰς γυναῖκας, καθὼς καὶ ὁ Χριστὸς ἠγάπησεν τὴν ἐκκλησίαν καὶ ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν ὑπὲρ αὐτῆς.”
Hoi andres, agapate tas gynaikas, kathōs kai ho Christos ēgapēsen tēn ekklēsian kai heauton paredōken hyper autēs.
Husbands.
Love your wives.
Just as Christ loved the church...
and gave Himself for her.
The command is ἀγαπᾶτε — agapate.
Love.
And Paul does not leave husbands free to invent their own definition of that love.
He gives them a Person to imitate.
Christ.
That changes everything.
Because Christ did not love His bride by crushing her.
He loved her by giving Himself for her.
He did not stand at Calvary demanding that His bride suffer for His comfort.
He suffered for her redemption.
He did not use His power to protect Himself from sacrifice.
He used His power in perfect obedience to the Father and willingly laid down His life.
That is the terrifying beauty of Ephesians 5.
Christian marriage does not give a husband permission to make himself the little god of his household.
There is already a Lord in the Christian home.
His name is Jesus.
And the husband himself bows before Him.
Before Paul ever reaches verse 25, Ephesians 5:21 places the household discussion under reverence for Christ: believers are called to submit to one another in the fear or reverence of Christ.
Then Paul speaks specifically to wives.
And then he speaks specifically to husbands.
We should not erase either instruction.
We should not rewrite Scripture to make it more comfortable for modern ears.
But neither should we isolate one instruction and weaponize it against the other person.
A husband who loves quoting his wife's responsibility while ignoring his own has not discovered biblical headship.
He has discovered selective reading.
Because when Paul turns to the husband, he does not merely say:
Be in charge.
He says:
Love her like Christ.
And what did Christ do?
“...gave himself for it.”
The Greek expression includes ἑαυτὸν παρέδωκεν — heauton paredōken.
He gave Himself up.
There is the shape of Christian husbandhood.
Self-giving.
Sacrifice.
Faithfulness.
Tenderness.
Holiness.
Truth.
Protection without possession.
Leadership without tyranny.
Strength without cruelty.
Conviction without humiliation.
Authority that remains accountable to Christ.
And love willing to pay a price.
Maybe that is uncomfortable.
It should be.
The Gospel has never existed merely to make our egos comfortable.
It crucifies them.
There may be a husband reading this who has never hit his wife.
Never cheated.
Never abandoned his family.
Never considered himself abusive.
But perhaps there are wounds in his home nobody sees.
The way the room changes when he becomes angry.
The silence everybody learns when Dad is irritated.
The wife who rehearses sentences before speaking because she is afraid of how he will react.
The apology he expects but rarely gives.
The decisions that are called “leadership” even though nobody else is allowed to speak.
The Scripture verses brought out during arguments like weapons.
The affection withheld to punish.
The sarcasm dismissed as humor.
The cold shoulder.
The contempt.
The constant correction.
The refusal to listen.
And perhaps the most dangerous sentence of all:
“I am the head of this house.”
Brother...
if you have to use Scripture to frighten your wife into remembering your position, something has gone terribly wrong.
Look again at Christ.
The One whom Scripture presents as Head of the Church is the same Christ who gave Himself for her.
His headship cannot be separated from His self-giving love.
Ephesians continues by saying that husbands should love their wives as their own bodies. Paul speaks of nourishing and cherishing, then brings the entire mystery back to Christ and His Church.
That means your wife's pain is not irrelevant because you won the argument.
Her dignity is not expendable because you believe your conclusion is correct.
Her voice is not your enemy.
Her weakness is not permission for exploitation.
Her disagreement does not erase her worth.
And her submission to Christ never gives you permission to become a substitute for Christ.
You are not her Savior.
Jesus is.
You are not her Holy Spirit.
You cannot bully someone into holiness.
You cannot intimidate someone into spiritual maturity.
You cannot control someone into becoming Christlike.
And you cannot call sinful domination “biblical leadership” simply because religious vocabulary has been wrapped around it.
Husbands, Scripture gives us something much harder than control.
It gives us a cross.
Imagine what could happen inside Christian homes if husbands became more concerned with resembling the crucified Christ than defending their privileges.
Imagine a husband saying:
“I was wrong.”
Without adding “but you...”
Imagine him putting down his phone and listening.
Imagine him praying with his wife instead of merely preaching at her.
Imagine him refusing pornography because covenant faithfulness matters more than secret gratification.
Imagine him serving when nobody applauds.
Imagine him becoming gentle without becoming weak.
Strong without becoming harsh.
Convicted without becoming self-righteous.
Imagine children growing up and thinking:
“When Dad talked about Jesus, I understood a little of what he meant because I watched him love Mom.”
That is a legacy.
Not perfection.
Christlikeness.
And before wives reading this begin forwarding it with a triumphant “SEE! I TOLD YOU!”...
there is something deeper happening here.
This passage is ultimately larger than husbands and wives.
Paul says so himself.
“This is a great mystery: but I speak concerning Christ and the church.” — Ephesians 5:32.
Marriage becomes a window.
Behind the window stands the Gospel.
Christ.
And His bride.
Suddenly this is not only a marriage article.
It is about you.
Because perhaps you have spent years believing that God relates to you the way controlling people did.
Maybe somebody used Christianity to dominate you.
Maybe Scripture was shouted instead of lived.
Maybe “submission” became a word that still makes your stomach tighten because someone used God's name to justify what God never authorized.
Maybe your earthly experience distorted your picture of your heavenly Bridegroom.
Then look at Jesus again.
Not the counterfeit.
Jesus.
Look at Him touching lepers.
Welcoming the broken.
Confronting hypocrisy.
Receiving repentant sinners.
Speaking truth.
Showing compassion.
And finally walking toward a cross.
Christ's love is not sentimental weakness.
It is holy love.
Truthful love.
Sacrificial love.
A love so serious about sin that He went to the cross.
A love so astonishing toward sinners that He went willingly.
That is why the Gospel is scandalous.
The innocent One suffered for the guilty.
The righteous One gave Himself for sinners.
The King wore thorns.
The Creator entered His creation.
The One who owed us nothing gave what we could never deserve.
Grace.
And perhaps the marriage you are looking at right now feels nothing like that.
Perhaps years of resentment have accumulated.
Perhaps conversations have become transactions.
Perhaps affection has become memory.
Perhaps the two of you sleep inches apart while emotionally living continents away.
Maybe she no longer believes your promises.
Maybe he no longer knows how to reach you.
Maybe there has been betrayal.
Maybe there are tears nobody knows about.
Maybe there are things that cannot be repaired by a romantic dinner and a Bible verse posted on Facebook.
The answer is not pretending.
The answer is not protecting an image while the marriage bleeds behind closed doors.

And where there is abuse, threats, coercion, or violence, seeking safety and qualified help is not a betrayal of biblical marriage. Scripture should never be used to demand that someone silently endure criminal or dangerous behavior.
But wherever repentance is possible, grace tells us something extraordinary:
The story does not have to end where the scandal happened.
That does not mean consequences disappear.
It does not mean trust magically returns overnight.
Forgiveness and reconciliation are not always identical processes.
Deep wounds may require time, pastoral wisdom, professional counseling, accountability, boundaries, restitution, and demonstrated change.
But Jesus specializes in resurrecting what sin said was finished.
This is where the husband who has failed must stop defending himself.
Brother, repentance does not begin with explaining why you did it.
Repentance begins when you stop running from the truth.
Maybe you have been controlling.
Repent.
Maybe you have been harsh.
Repent.
Maybe pornography has been living secretly in your marriage.
Bring it into the light.
Maybe another woman has occupied emotional territory that belonged inside your covenant.
End it.
Maybe pride has made “I'm sorry” feel impossible.
Say it anyway.
Maybe you know a hundred Bible verses but your wife rarely experiences the fruit of the Spirit when she disagrees with you.
Then stop using your knowledge of Scripture as evidence that you are spiritually healthy.
Let Scripture examine you.
Jesus did not call men merely to know verses.
He called us to follow Him.
And following Jesus eventually brings every man's pride to a cross.
There is something almost unbearable about Paul's standard:
“...as Christ also loved the church.”
Who can measure up to that?
None of us.
That is precisely why husbands need the Gospel too.
This passage is not a ladder by which men climb toward self-righteousness.
It exposes our need for grace.
We fail.
We become selfish.
We become impatient.
We become defensive.
We carry wounds into marriage and sometimes turn those wounds into weapons.
But the same Christ whose love exposes us is the Christ whose blood cleanses repentant sinners.
The husband kneeling before Jesus does not have to pretend he has never failed.
He has to stop pretending he does not need grace.
Maybe your wife needs to hear something from you tonight that she has waited years to hear.
Not:
“You misunderstood me.”
Not:
“You made me angry.”
Not:
“If you had submitted...”
Maybe she needs to hear:
“I sinned against you.”
“I was wrong.”
“What I did was not Christlike.”
“I have used anger where I should have shown gentleness.”
“I have demanded from you what I was unwilling to demand from myself.”
“Please forgive me.”
“I want Jesus to change me.”
And then...
do not make those words another performance.
Live your repentance.
Let your changed behavior become the apology's evidence.
Let humility become visible.
Let accountability become normal.
Let Christ become more important than protecting your reputation.
And wives...
please hear this carefully too.
A husband loving sacrificially does not mean a wife becomes his judge, master, or controller.
The answer to male domination is not female domination.
Christian marriage is not a competition to determine who gets to become the household tyrant.
It is covenant life under Jesus Christ.
Both husband and wife belong to Him.
Both need grace.
Both are sinners.
Both are called to holiness.
Both possess God-given dignity.
And both ultimately answer to Christ.
The Gospel does not merely rearrange who gets the throne.
The Gospel reminds us that the throne was never ours.
Jesus is Lord.
Maybe that is the sentence our marriages desperately need again.
Jesus is Lord.
Not husband.
Not wife.
Not culture.
Not tradition.
Not ego.
Jesus.
And when Jesus is truly Lord, masculinity no longer needs cruelty to prove strength.
Leadership no longer needs intimidation to establish authority.
Marriage no longer needs appearances to hide decay.
Repentance becomes possible because grace is real.
Forgiveness becomes imaginable because we ourselves have been forgiven.
Sacrifice stops looking like defeat because our Savior conquered through a cross.
That is Christianity.
A King with scars.
A Savior who serves.
A Bridegroom who gives Himself for His bride.
A grave that could not keep Him.
A sinner who can come home.
A marriage that may have chapters filled with failure but does not have to let failure write the final sentence.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
If this exposed something in you, do not rush past the discomfort.
Sit with God.
Pray.
Open Ephesians 5 and read the whole passage rather than the single sentence you find easiest to quote.
Ask the Holy Spirit:
“Where have I demanded Christlikeness from my spouse while excusing its absence in me?”
And if your heart is convicted, do not hide behind religious language.
And if you have been pretending everything is okay while quietly falling apart, maybe today is the day to stop hiding.
Not because strangers need your private details.
You do not owe the internet your wounds.
But sometimes three honest words are enough to say:
“I need my brothers and sisters in Christ to stand with me.”
And if you know a husband who needs this message, do not send it as a weapon.
Send it as an invitation.

If you know a young man preparing for marriage, tag him—not to shame him, but because he deserves to learn before marriage what some men discover only after they have wounded the person they promised to love.
Come back to it after the argument.
Come back when pride begins whispering.
Come back when you need to remember what Christian strength looks like.
It does not.
It cannot.
Scripture does not give us the right to make that claim.
We are saved by grace, and Christian giving is to come from the heart rather than compulsion.
And there is something else we want believers to know.

If this ministry feeds you spiritually, helps you return to Scripture, encourages repentance, strengthens marriages, reaches struggling believers, or helps somebody discover the grace of Jesus, prayerfully consider standing with us.
And whether you ever give financially or not, you can still help carry the message.
Send it privately to the couple who needs hope.
Because somewhere tonight there is a husband who thinks winning the argument means he has won.
There is a wife quietly wondering whether God sees her tears.
There is a marriage sitting one conversation away from either another wound or the beginning of repentance.
There is a man who needs to discover that biblical strength is not demonstrated by how completely he can control another human being.
It is revealed in how completely he is willing to surrender himself to Jesus.
And there is a cross standing at the center of Christianity forever answering the question:
“What does love look like?”
It looks like Christ.
Giving Himself.
For His bride.
So husbands...
before asking whether your wife is following the biblical command given to her, stand before Jesus and ask the question Scripture places directly before you:
Does the way I love her make it easier for her to recognize something of Christ?
Because one day the arguments will stop.
The house will become quiet.
The children will grow older.
The photographs will fade.
The titles will disappear.
And all the little kingdoms we fought so desperately to control will pass away.
But Jesus will still be Lord.
So love her while you have breath.
Repent while your heart can still be softened.
Forgive while there is still time to embrace.
Speak truth without cruelty.
Lead without domination.
Protect without possessing.
Serve without keeping score.
And when you fail...
run back to the Savior whose grace is greater than your worst chapter.

Because the strongest husband is not the man who makes everyone in his house bow to him—it is the man who bows so completely to Jesus that his family begins to recognize the Savior in the way he loves.
